lei_day.label: Lei Day
lei_day.intro: Hawaii's flowery answer to the first of May: people string, wear and give away leis, and the whole day smells of plumeria. A garland says hello, goodbye, congratulations and thank you all at once.
funFacts: Writer Don Blanding suggested a lei holiday in 1928; Grace Tower Warren added the slogan "May Day is Lei Day".
Every Hawaiian island has its own lei colour and plant, from Oahu's golden ilima to Kauai's purple mokihana berries.
Leis are woven, braided or strung with a needle, and are traditionally returned to nature rather than thrown in the bin.

ukulele_day.label: National Play Your Ukulele Day
ukulele_day.intro: Four nylon strings, a body the size of a shoebox and almost no way to sound gloomy. Today the idea is simply to pick one up and strum, whether you know three chords or thirty.
funFacts: The ukulele grew up in 1880s Hawaii out of the machete, a small guitar brought over by cabinet makers from Madeira.
The Hawaiian name roughly translates as "jumping flea", said to describe the way a player's fingers dart about.
A standard ukulele is tuned G-C-E-A, and its top string sits higher in pitch than the one below it.

two_different_colored_shoes_day.label: Two Different Colored Shoes Day
two_different_colored_shoes_day.intro: Wear one red shoe and one blue one and see who notices. A tiny, harmless act of rebellion against the idea that everything has to match.
funFacts: The oldest known leather shoe, found in a cave at Areni in Armenia, is roughly 5,500 years old.
Ötzi the Iceman walked in shoes of deer and bear hide, insulated with grass stuffed between the layers.
Shoes shaped separately for left and right feet only became normal in the 19th century; before that many were "straights".

star_wars_day.label: Star Wars Day
star_wars_day.intro: "May the Fourth be with you" — one pun turned a date into a global fan holiday. Marathons, costumes and lightsaber duels in living rooms everywhere.
funFacts: The earliest known use of the pun was a 1979 newspaper advert congratulating Margaret Thatcher on her election win.
Disney has officially marked the day since 2013, often using it to launch new Star Wars releases.
Fans follow it up with "Revenge of the Fifth" on 5 May, a day for the villains of the saga.

cartoonists_day.label: National Cartoonists Day
cartoonists_day.intro: A tip of the hat to the people who can tell a whole story in three panels. Newspaper strips, cartoons and comic books all started with someone at a desk with a pen.
funFacts: Richard F. Outcault's Yellow Kid, from 1895, is one of the first newspaper comic characters — and gave the "yellow press" its name.
Charles M. Schulz drew nearly 18,000 Peanuts strips over almost 50 years, every single one by his own hand.
Rube Goldberg, whose name now means any absurdly complicated machine, won a Pulitzer Prize for cartooning in 1948.

crepe_suzette_day.label: National Crêpe Suzette Day
crepe_suzette_day.intro: Thin pancakes, warm orange butter, a splash of liqueur and a brief burst of flame at the table. Dessert as a small piece of theatre.
funFacts: The sauce is built from butter, sugar, orange juice and zest, then flambéed with an orange liqueur such as Grand Marnier.
Legend credits a teenage waiter in 1890s Monte Carlo with setting the sauce alight by accident; food historians are sceptical.
Crêpes are poured so thin that a good cook can spread the batter across the pan in a single wrist movement.

mural_day.label: National Mural Day
mural_day.intro: A day for the art you cannot hang on a wall, because it is the wall. Murals turn firewalls, underpasses and gable ends into something worth looking up at.
funFacts: Mexican muralism made the form famous in the 1920s, with Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros painting public buildings.
Berlin's East Side Gallery stretches 1,316 metres along a surviving stretch of the Wall and is one of the longest open-air galleries.
Painting on walls is the oldest art we know: the cave images at Lascaux are roughly 17,000 years old.

world_donkey_day.label: World Donkey Day
world_donkey_day.intro: A day for the patient, long-eared workmate that has carried people and their luggage for thousands of years — and is usually far cleverer than its reputation suggests.
funFacts: Donkeys were domesticated in north-east Africa some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, most likely by herding peoples in Nubia.
A donkey's bray carries for more than three kilometres, handy for keeping in touch across open desert country.
What looks like stubbornness is caution: a donkey stops to think about danger instead of bolting the way a horse does.

lost_sock_memorial_day.label: Lost Sock Memorial Day
lost_sock_memorial_day.intro: A cheerfully silly farewell to every sock that went into the wash as one of a pair and came out alone. Time to let the survivor go, or give it a mismatched new life.
funFacts: The word sock comes from the Latin soccus, a light slipper worn by comic actors on the Roman stage.
Knitted Egyptian socks with a split toe, made to be worn with sandals, survive from roughly 300-500 AD.
William Lee invented the stocking frame in 1589 — the first knitting machine, built specifically to make socks faster.

shrimp_day.label: National Shrimp Day
shrimp_day.intro: Grilled, fried, in a curry or straight from the pan with garlic: shrimp are one of the fastest routes from kitchen to table. A day to enjoy them without ceremony.
funFacts: Shrimp turn pink when cooked because heat frees the pigment astaxanthin from the proteins that were hiding it.
The pistol shrimp snaps its claw so fast that the collapsing bubble makes one of the loudest sounds in the ocean.
Cleaner shrimp run "cleaning stations" on reefs where fish line up to have parasites picked off.

twilight_zone_day.label: National Twilight Zone Day
twilight_zone_day.intro: A day for the anthology series that made the twist ending famous. Half an hour, one strange idea, and a closing line that leaves you staring at the ceiling.
funFacts: Rod Serling created the show and wrote or co-wrote 92 of its 156 episodes between 1959 and 1964.
He chose science fiction partly because network censors let him say things there that a realistic drama could not.
The phrase "the twilight zone" left the screen and became everyday shorthand for anything unsettlingly odd.

limerick_day.label: Limerick Day
limerick_day.intro: Five lines, a bouncing rhythm, a rhyme scheme of AABBA and a punchline that should really not be taken seriously. Today the challenge is to write one yourself.
funFacts: The date is Edward Lear's birthday: the English writer and illustrator was born on 12 May 1812.
Lear did not invent the limerick, but his 1846 Book of Nonsense made the form famous far beyond Britain.
Lines one, two and five rhyme and are long; lines three and four rhyme with each other and are short.

world_cocktail_day.label: World Cocktail Day
world_cocktail_day.intro: The birthday of a word: on this date in 1806 a New York paper printed the first known definition of a cocktail. Reason enough to shake, stir and clink a glass.
funFacts: On 13 May 1806 The Balance and Columbian Repository defined a cocktail as spirits, sugar, water and bitters.
That description is essentially the recipe for what we now call an Old Fashioned.
Jerry Thomas published the first proper bartender's guide, How to Mix Drinks, in 1862.

dance_like_a_chicken_day.label: Dance Like a Chicken Day
dance_like_a_chicken_day.intro: Beaks, flapping wings, wiggle, four claps — the dance nobody admits to knowing and everybody joins in anyway. A day to give in gracefully.
funFacts: Swiss accordionist Werner Thomas wrote the tune in Davos in the 1950s and called it Der Ententanz, the duck dance.
It became the "chicken" dance in Tulsa in 1981, when an Oktoberfest could find a chicken costume but no duck one.
More than 140 versions have been recorded, adding up to tens of millions of records pressed worldwide.

chocolate_chip_day.label: National Chocolate Chip Day
chocolate_chip_day.intro: The small brown lumps that turn plain dough into a cookie worth queueing for. Today they get the credit rather than the biscuit around them.
funFacts: Ruth Wakefield of the Toll House Inn in Massachusetts put chopped chocolate into cookie dough in the 1930s.
Nestlé printed her recipe on its chocolate wrappers and began selling ready-made morsels in 1939.
Baking chips hold their shape in the oven because they contain less cocoa butter than a bar of eating chocolate.

international_day_of_light.label: International Day of Light
international_day_of_light.intro: A UNESCO day for everything light does: sunrise, rainbows, fibre-optic cables and laser surgery. The date marks the moment the laser stopped being theory.
funFacts: On 16 May 1960 Theodore Maiman ran the first working laser, using a synthetic ruby crystal and a flash lamp.
Laser is an acronym: light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.
Sunlight needs about eight minutes and twenty seconds to travel from the Sun to your window.

mushroom_hunting_day.label: National Mushroom Hunting Day
mushroom_hunting_day.intro: Basket, knife, sturdy boots and a slow walk with your eyes on the forest floor. Mushroom hunting is half a hobby, half a treasure hunt — with a strict rule about never eating anything you cannot name.
funFacts: Fungi are their own kingdom, and genetically they sit closer to animals than to plants.
The mushroom you pick is only the fruiting body; the actual organism is a web of threads spread through the soil.
One honey fungus in Oregon covers several square kilometres and counts as one of the largest organisms on Earth.

international_museum_day.label: International Museum Day
international_museum_day.intro: Thousands of museums open their doors with special tours, late openings and free entry. A day to walk into the building you always mean to visit.
funFacts: The International Council of Museums has coordinated the day since 1977, each year under a new theme.
By 2017 some 36,000 museums in 156 countries were taking part.
The Ashmolean in Oxford, opened in 1683, is often called the first university museum open to the public.

devils_food_cake_day.label: National Devil's Food Cake Day
devils_food_cake_day.intro: Dark, damp and unapologetically chocolatey — the wicked twin of the pale, airy angel food cake. A day for a very large slice.
funFacts: Recipes under the name devil's food appear in American cookbooks from around the turn of the twentieth century.
The name is a joke about its opposite: angel food cake is white, fat-free and feather-light.
Natural cocoa reacting with baking soda can give the crumb a reddish tint — the same effect behind red velvet cake.

world_bee_day.label: World Bee Day
world_bee_day.intro: A UN day for the small striped workers behind a huge share of what ends up on our plates. Beekeepers open hives, schools plant flowers, and honey gets eaten.
funFacts: The date honours Anton Janša, a pioneer of modern beekeeping, baptised in Slovenia on 20 May 1734.
Karl von Frisch decoded the waggle dance, which tells hive mates the direction and distance of food, and shared a Nobel Prize in 1973.
One worker bee produces roughly a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her entire life.

international_tea_day.label: International Tea Day
international_tea_day.intro: A UN day for the world's second-most-drunk liquid after plain water. Green, black, oolong or white — all of it starts on the same bush.
funFacts: Green, oolong and black tea all come from Camellia sinensis; only the degree of oxidation differs.
Chinese legend credits the mythical emperor Shennong with discovering tea in 2737 BC.
Turkey drinks more tea per person than anywhere else, well ahead of the countries usually associated with the habit.

world_goth_day.label: World Goth Day
world_goth_day.intro: Black lace, dry humour and a soundtrack of guitars in minor keys. A day for a subculture that has been cheerfully misunderstood for forty years.
funFacts: The day began in the UK in 2009, sparked by a BBC Radio 6 Music week devoted to musical subcultures.
Bauhaus's 1979 single Bela Lugosi's Dead is widely treated as the starting pistol for gothic rock.
Leipzig's Wave-Gotik-Treffen draws tens of thousands of visitors and turns the whole city black each spring.

world_turtle_day.label: World Turtle Day
world_turtle_day.intro: A day for one of the calmest designs in the animal kingdom: an animal that carries its own house and is in absolutely no hurry.
funFacts: The shell is not a shed-able case: the upper part is fused with the turtle's spine and ribs.
In many species the nest temperature decides whether the hatchlings are male or female.
Turtles have been around since the Triassic, which makes their lineage well over 200 million years old.

escargot_day.label: National Escargot Day
escargot_day.intro: Snails baked in garlic and parsley butter, eaten with special tongs and a tiny fork. Strange the first time, hard to give up afterwards.
funFacts: The classic Burgundy version uses Helix pomatia and a butter beaten together with garlic, parsley and shallots.
The dish has its own cutlery: a dimpled plate, spring-loaded tongs and a narrow two-pronged fork.
A snail eats with a radula, a rasping tongue carrying thousands of microscopic teeth.

towel_day.label: Towel Day
towel_day.intro: Fans of Douglas Adams carry a towel around all day, because the Hitchhiker's Guide insists it is the most massively useful thing an interstellar traveller can own.
funFacts: The first Towel Day was held on 25 May 2001, two weeks after Douglas Adams died.
In the books, anyone still holding their towel is assumed to have their whole life under control.
Astronauts Samantha Cristoforetti and Tim Peake have both celebrated the day aboard the International Space Station.

world_dracula_day.label: World Dracula Day
world_dracula_day.intro: The anniversary of the novel that gave the world its most famous vampire. A day for capes, castles and reading by candlelight.
funFacts: Bram Stoker's Dracula went on sale in London in late May 1897, bound in yellow cloth with red lettering.
The manuscript carried the working title The Un-Dead until shortly before publication.
The book is told entirely through diary entries, letters, newspaper cuttings and a ship's log.

grape_popsicle_day.label: National Grape Popsicle Day
grape_popsicle_day.intro: Purple, sticky, gone in five minutes and guaranteed to stain your tongue. The ice lolly is summer's cheapest pleasure, and today it gets its own date.
funFacts: Eleven-year-old Frank Epperson left a drink with a stirring stick outside overnight in 1905 and found it frozen solid.
He patented the frozen treat in 1924, almost twenty years after that accident.
He called it an Epsicle; his children insisted on "Pop's sicle", and the shorter name stuck.

hamburger_day.label: National Hamburger Day
hamburger_day.intro: Bun, patty, whatever you like in between. Few dishes have travelled further or been argued about more, and today the only job is to eat one.
funFacts: The name travels back to Hamburg via the "Hamburg steak" that German emigrants took to the United States.
Several American towns claim to have served the first burger in a bun, and none of them can prove it.
The 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis is often credited with introducing the sandwich to a mass audience.

paperclip_day.label: National Paperclip Day
paperclip_day.intro: A bent piece of wire that has outlasted almost every office gadget invented since. Cheap, silent, endlessly reusable — and quietly heroic.
funFacts: The familiar double-oval Gem clip was never patented; it simply appeared in Britain in the late 19th century.
Norwegian Johan Vaaler patented a wire clip in 1899, though his design lacked the Gem's two full loops.
Under German occupation, Norwegians wore paperclips on their lapels as a silent sign of solidarity.

potato_day.label: International Day of Potato
potato_day.intro: A UN day for the lumpy, unglamorous tuber that feeds more people than almost anything else. Boiled, mashed, roasted or fried — nobody agrees which is best.
funFacts: The potato was domesticated in the Andes of South America thousands of years ago and reached Europe in the 16th century.
Peru alone holds thousands of native varieties, in colours ranging from cream to deep purple.
Potatoes were grown aboard a Space Shuttle mission in 1995, one of the first food crops cultivated in orbit.

world_parrot_day.label: World Parrot Day
world_parrot_day.intro: Loud, brilliantly coloured and far too clever for their own good. A day for the birds that will happily outlive, outwit and out-argue their owners.
funFacts: The day was launched by the World Parrot Trust in 2004.
Parrots do not have vocal cords; they shape sounds with the syrinx and a remarkably muscular tongue.
Alex, an African grey studied by Irene Pepperberg, learned to use more than a hundred words meaningfully.
